extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, critics, and practitioners of poetry/drama and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Aristotle’s principles for composing and evaluating poetry and drama (as presented and discussed by S. H. Butcher). Covers imitation, universality, plot, character, tragedy/comedy devices, unities, katharsis, metre, and the aesthetic vs. moral purpose of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as an aesthetic term
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ as the common characteristic of the Fine Arts: a current phrase interpreted anew by Aristotle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle redefines 'imitation' away from literal copying toward the artistic representation of human life; treat imitation as the artful rendering of types, actions, passions and character rather than mechanical replication. Anti-pattern: reading ‘imitation’ as mere facsimile of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of aesthetic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of aesthetic imitation are human Character, Passions, Action (ἤθη, πάθη, πράξεις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works should aim to represent character, emotion, and action (ethos, pathē, praxis). Examples: tragedy focuses on actions that elicit pity and fear. Use these categories to decide what to depict and foreground in a scene or plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work of Art is a likeness (ὁμοίωμα), not symbolical representation (σημεῖον)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of Art is a likeness (ὁμοίωμα) of an end, not a symbolical representation (σημεῖον) of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for an aesthetic semblance that shows the essential form or type of its subject; do not rely on mere symbolic or allegorical shorthand. The work reproduces its original as presented to the imagination/phantasy rather than as a literal transcription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art expresses the universal (τὸ καθόλου)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitative or Fine Art in its highest manifestation, namely Poetry, is an expression of the universal element (τὸ καθόλου) in human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry/drama abstracts from particulars to reveal universal human truths—characters and incidents should exemplify general types. Evaluate works by their success in making the universal perceptible through particular representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs historical fact (probabilities and possibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is not a reproduction of empirical fact: the 'probabilities' and 'possibilities' of Poetry contrasted with those of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic plausibility (what might or ought to be) is more important than factual accuracy. Acceptable: 'probable impossibilities' that illuminate truth; Unacceptable: improbably impossible events that break the internal logic. Use probability/possibility to judge verisimilitude in plot and character motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry excludes the rule of Chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry excludes the rule of Chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on pure chance to resolve plots or effect reversals; plot outcomes should arise from necessity or probability within the story world. Anti-pattern: deus ex machina that depends on random coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of Fine Art: pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Fine Art is pleasure. Its lower forms afford the pleasure of a pastime (παιδιά); its higher forms, that noble enjoyment (διαγωγή) which belongs to supreme happiness (εὐδαιμονία).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with the aim of producing aesthetic pleasure appropriate to the work’s level: entertainment vs. noble enjoyment. Consider audience pleasure (hearer/spectator) as the primary telos; avoid gratuitous elements that do not contribute to the audience’s aesthetic enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of Tragedy: katharsis of pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic Katharsis of pity and fear: tragedy produces pity and fear leading to a katharsis—an emotional relief or clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should build pity and fear through credible actions and reversals, culminating in a cleansing or clarification of those emotions. Consider both emotional arousal and their proper resolution/clarification when designing tragic sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the primary Unity: tragedy as an organic whole with 'beginning, middle, and end'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plots with a single, coherent causal action that moves from a clear beginning through development to an inevitable end. Evaluate by whether incidents cohere to form a unified plot; avoid fragmented, episodic structures that lack causal unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time and Unity of Place (secondary and misapplied rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Time: noted in Greek practice and later made into a rule; Unity of Place nowhere mentioned in Aristotle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fetishize strict temporal or spatial coincident limits; treat time and place as instruments of idealisation. Emphasize Unity of Action over mechanical adherence to time/place unities. Beware of elevating incidental unities above structural unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero / protagonist requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal type of protagonist is deduced by Aristotle from the function of Tragedy to produce pity and fear. Several types of excluded characters: blameless goodness, signal villainy; protagonist should be σπουδαῖος.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose protagonists who are serious/respectable (spoudaios) but not perfectly virtuous nor monstrous villains—figures whose fall evokes pity and fear. Examples of problematic exclusions include Antigone and Clytemnestra under some strict readings; be ready to qualify rules when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (ἁμαρτία) as tragic error
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s ideal protagonist involves ἁμαρτία — an error or fault which leads to reversal and suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground tragic reversal in a protagonist’s error/limitation rather than moral wickedness alone. Use hamartia to produce sympathetic recognition of human fallibility. Modern readings may enlarge the sense of hamartia beyond a single technical mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (μῦθος) as the primary element; plot devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (μῦθος) or Action is the primary element according to Aristotle: it is the 'soul' of tragedy and includes reversal (περιπέτεια) and recognition (ἀναγνώρισις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize constructing a coherent sequence of events (plot) that produces catharsis. Employ peripeteia and anagnorisis as powerful mechanisms for effective tragic structure; judge works primarily on plot integrity and causal necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character is constituted by Ethos and Dianoia but subordinate to Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethos and Dianoia constitute Character in its largest sense, but Aristotle subordinates character to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop character traits and thought (beliefs, intentions) insofar as they serve and arise from action. Avoid making character description an end in itself where it undermines plot causality; reconcile deep characterisation with the primacy of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability/possibility vs improbabilities (poetic plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senses of the 'possible' and 'improbable' in poetry: permissible are probabilities and possibilities; avoid improbable impossibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept imaginative departures from fact only if they remain psychologically and narratively plausible. 'Probable impossibilities' that illuminate general truth may be allowed; blatant logical impossibilities that break internal consistency are faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις) and Reversal (περιπέτεια)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition and Reversal are essential structural devices for producing catharsis and unifying plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-timed recognition and reversal to convert ignorance into knowledge and to shift the action’s direction credibly. Evaluate these devices by their inevitability and causal fit within the plot (not by novelty alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse and metre as elements of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse as an element of Poetry: metre and verbal medium are part of poetic imitation; 'poet' includes musician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider metre, rhythm, and musicality integral to poetic effect. For dramatic poetry, blend verbal metre with musical/dance elements where appropriate. Evaluate how formal features (metre, rhythm) enhance the representation of character/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Music, Dance, and Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, with Music and Dancing as forming a single group; the musical Katharsis is noted in the Politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat music and dance (including chorus) as co-equal modes that intensify affect and katharsis. Use them to shape emotional texture and to underscore universal themes. Anti-pattern: marginalizing musical elements when they are integral to the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s generalising power
rubrics_metrics.description: The generalising power of Comedy: comedy idealises life by generalisation and creates personified ideals; humour operates differently from pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comedy aim to represent typical human follies and types, using names and caricature to reveal generalities; balance sportive generalisation with insight. Evaluate comedy by its success in universalising the ludicrous without descending into mere insult or caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation versus individualisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Senses of the word 'idealise.' Tragedy and Comedy idealise life in different ways: tragedy idealises persons; comedy produces personified ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work’s aim is to present an ideal (universal type) or to represent unique individuals. Modern drama often increases emphasis on individualised character—adjust expectations accordingly when applying Aristotelian criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Fine Art and Useful Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The theoretic distinction between Fine and Useful Art first established by Aristotle; 'Art imitates Nature' specially in reference to Useful Art, which follows Nature’s methods and supplies her defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether a craft is judged for utility or aesthetic universality. Apply different evaluative measures: utility and functionality for useful arts; universality, unity, and expressive power for fine arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and Morality: aesthetic over didactic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes the educational from the aesthetic function of Poetry: his critical estimates of Poetry rest on purely aesthetic grounds, though some rules reflect moral considerations (e.g., tragic characters must be σπουδαῖοι).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art primarily by aesthetic criteria (unity, imitation of the universal, katharsis) rather than moral instruction, while noting that moral qualities of characters can affect aesthetic success. Anti-pattern: conflating moral approval with artistic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem as organic whole / unity and 'whole' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of a poem as an organism; the ideal unity and 'whole'—parts must contribute to the unity of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that episodes, scenes, and characters function together to sustain the central action; remove or alter parts that do not contribute to the organism. Use 'beginning, middle, end' as structural test for organic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination/phantasy mediates representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of Art reproduces its original not as it is in itself, but as it is presented in sensuous form to the 'phantasy' (φαντασία).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ imaginative rendering—select sensory and formal means to present the universal through particular images. Evaluate whether the work’s imaginative shaping brings out the intended type or universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as philosophically higher than History
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'a more philosophical and a higher thing than History': it represents the universal through the particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging works, value the capacity to convey general truths about human life via crafted incidents rather than mere chronicle of events. Assess whether a poem/drama raises understanding of human universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage scenery and architecture (scope of imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architecture is not included among the Imitative Arts; scenery and stage setting are idealised matters treated differently from other imitative arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate architectural realism with poetic imitation—scenery should serve the representation and idealisation of action rather than literal duplication. Evaluate scenic elements by how they support the universalizing aims of the work.
